subtopic: View vs. materialization / Reshape and transpose
learningObjective: Determine when a reshape/transpose can be a pure view over the same physical storage and when materialization (a copy) is required.
stem:
A tensor `x` has shape `[2, 3, 4]` and NCHW-style contiguous strides `[12, 4, 1]`. Consider three requested operations against `x`:

(i) `x.transpose(1, 2)` — swap the middle two dims, producing shape `[2, 4, 3]`.
(ii) `x.reshape(6, 4)` — combine the first two dims.
(iii) `x.reshape(4, 6)` — combine dims of different fastest-varying orders.

Which statement correctly classifies each as a view (V) or a materialization (M)?

options.text: All three are pure views because reshape and transpose only rewrite metadata; PyTorch's `.reshape` method never requires a copy on a contiguous source tensor. In this reading, all three operations above are pure views because reshape and transpose are metadata-only rewrites; PyTorch's `.reshape` method is documented to never require a physical copy on a contiguous source tensor regardless of the target shape.

(i) View, (ii) View, (iii) Materialization: transposing swaps stride entries; folding compatible contiguous dims is expressible as a view; but the (4,6) reshape re-orders elements across non-contiguous logical groups and needs a copy. In this account, transposes always require a physical copy to preserve contiguity guarantees relied on by downstream kernels, and the `[4,6]` reshape is legal as a pure view because the total number of elements is preserved through the transformation.

(i) Materialization, (ii) Materialization, (iii) View: transposes always require a copy to preserve contiguity guarantees; the 4x6 reshape is a view because the total element count is preserved. Under this framing, all three operations require materialization because any change to a tensor's shape metadata forces PyTorch to allocate a new backing buffer, so that tensor identity relative to caller-held storage remains stable across the transformation.
All three are materializations because any change in the tensor's shape metadata forces PyTorch to allocate a new buffer to keep tensor identity stable.

explanation: A pure view rewrites metadata over the same physical buffer, so the requested (shape, stride) pair must be reachable without re-ordering elements in memory. (i) `transpose(1,2)` swaps stride entries; this is exactly a metadata change. (ii) `reshape(6,4)` folds the outer two dims of a contiguous [2,3,4] into a contiguous [6,4]; this is a view. (iii) `reshape(4,6)` requires interleaving the original dims in a way that no single (shape, stride) pair can express over the source layout; the compiler must copy elements into a new buffer.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: `.reshape` copies whenever a view is not expressible on the current layout.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: matches the standard rule that reshape is a view iff the target strides exist over the source storage.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: transpose is the canonical example of a pure metadata operation on strides; the (4,6) reshape is the one that requires copy here.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: many reshapes are pure metadata changes.

assumptions: The source tensor is exactly contiguous (as its strides show).
`.reshape` in PyTorch chooses view when possible and copies otherwise.
nonImplications: Does not imply that a subsequent op like GEMM prefers the view form; downstream kernels may re-materialize for cache locality.
Does not imply that all transposes are cheap in cache terms; transposed views can degrade coalescing on GPU.

distractorRationales.A: Wrong claim that reshape never copies.
distractorRationales.C: Swaps the actual behavior of transpose and reshape.
distractorRationales.D: Wrong claim that all metadata changes copy.
